beginner: Jalapeno likes rich, well-drained soil that warms up well in the sun, because peppers barely grow until the ground is warm. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives the plant the head start it wants. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, since soggy roots invite disease.
seasoned: Jalapeno wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and like all peppers it grows slowly until the ground is truly warm. A sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay, since a pepper set into cold soil simply sits there until it heats up. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Steady, even moisture in a freely draining soil is the target: soggy roots stall the plant and invite the Phytophthora blight peppers are prone to, while a mild, deliberate water pull late in the season can actually sharpen a hot pepper's heat.

beginner: Jalapeno likes slightly acidic soil, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best. Peppers are not too fussy and will grow a bit outside this band, but an inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand and whether to add lime or sulfur before planting.
seasoned: Jalapeno grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, with Clemson placing the sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5 where the nutrients peppers need stay most available. It tolerates a somewhat wider band, roughly 5.5 to 7.5, and in fact chile is grown successfully on the neutral-to-alkaline soils common across the interior West, though uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as soil turns strongly alkaline, showing as yellowing between the veins of younger leaves. Most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target; a soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant and tells you whether to lime an acid soil or add sulfur to an alkaline one.

beginner: Jalapeno does not need heavy feeding. Mix a modest amount of a balanced fertilizer, or one a little lower in nitrogen like 5-10-10, into the soil before you plant. Then wait: once the first little peppers have set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer, and again during picking. Going heavy on nitrogen too early gives you a big leafy plant with hardly any peppers, so save the feeding for after fruit starts forming.
seasoned: Jalapeno is a moderate feeder, not a heavy one. Follow a soil test, or work a modest amount of a balanced-to-low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen once the first fruits have set, about three to four weeks after planting, and again during harvest. Hold the nitrogen back before fruit set: too much early on drives a big leafy plant with few flowers, the single most common reason a pepper looks lush but sets almost no pods. Pair feeding with steady moisture, and note that a mild, deliberate water and nitrogen pull as the crop ripens tends to concentrate a hot pepper's heat.

beginner: Your jalapeno is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer to keep it producing.
seasoned: Your jalapeno has set its first fruit, a good time to side-dress with nitrogen to keep production going through the season.

beginner: Use a balanced or lower-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed once fruit sets. Do not overdo the nitrogen early or you get all leaves and few peppers.
seasoned: A balanced or slightly low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress (for example calcium nitrate, 15.5-0-0) once fruit sets. Avoid heavy nitrogen before fruit set, which gives leaf at the expense of flowers and pods.

beginner: Mix a modest amount of balanced fertilizer, or a few inches of compost, into the soil before planting. Then, once fruit has set, scratch a nitrogen fertilizer into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in, repeating once during the picking season.
seasoned: Clemson suggests side-dressing about 5 pounds of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 1000 square feet three to four weeks after planting and repeating during harvest, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in. At planting, a light complete feeding or a few inches of compost is plenty for this moderate feeder.

beginner: The most useful jalapeno companions are easy neighbors like basil, which enjoys the same warm, sunny, evenly watered conditions, plus a ring of marigolds or nasturtiums to lure aphids and flea beetles away. Bush beans add a little nitrogen. The one rule that really matters is to keep jalapeno away from tomatoes, eggplant, and potatoes, which are close relatives and share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most jalapeno companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. Basil is the classic pepper neighbor, an easy match since both are warm-season crops that want the same sun and water, and a border of nasturtium or marigold is the usual deflector, drawing or repelling the aphids and flea beetles that trouble peppers. Bush beans fix a little nitrogen the moderately feeding plant appreciates. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep jalapeno away from its Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, eggplant, and potatoes, which share its full pest and disease complex, including the aphid-borne mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, and bacterial spot.

beginner: Basil is the traditional friend of peppers and an easy pairing, since both love the same warm, sunny, evenly watered spot. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
seasoned: The classic pepper companion in garden tradition, said to support growth and flavor and to help deter some pests. Beyond tradition, it is simply a compatible neighbor: both are warm-season crops with matched sun, heat, and water needs, so they thrive together.

beginner: Bush beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that peppers can use. A good, traditional neighbor.
seasoned: Legumes fix a little nitrogen the moderately feeding pepper appreciates. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near peppers to lure aphids and flea beetles away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
seasoned: Often planted around solanaceous crops as a trap and deterrent for aphids and flea beetles, drawing them off the peppers. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-pepper effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for peppers, traditionally grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but a cheerful, low-risk choice.
seasoned: A long-standing companion tradition near peppers; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented nematode-suppressive effects, though the interplanted marigold-pepper pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

beginner: Keep jalapeno away from tomatoes, eggplant, and potatoes. They are all close relatives that share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share jalapeno's full pest and disease complex, including aphids and the mosaic viruses they carry, flea beetle, hornworm, Phytophthora blight, bacterial spot, and anthracnose. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 to 4 year cycle.

beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: Tiny soft green or black insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. Worse, aphids spread the viruses that stunt and mottle pepper plants.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and leaf undersides, curling and yellowing the leaves, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. On peppers the greater damage is indirect: aphids are the main vectors of the mosaic viruses that mottle and distort pepper foliage and stunt the plant, so aphid control is largely virus prevention.

beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft growth from too much nitrogen. As they move around they spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid (Myzus persicae), that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on soft, over-fertilized growth. As they probe plant to plant they transmit cucumber mosaic and other viruses, which is why they head the pepper pest list.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control; reflective mulch deters them from young plants.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, use reflective mulch on young plants, and let helpful insects do their work. Pull out any badly virus-stunted plants so aphids do not carry the disease onward.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, use reflective mulch on young plants, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Remove virus-infected plants promptly, since aphids spread the disease from them.

beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature. Damage is most severe on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred; established plants tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.

beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and target young plants early in the season.
seasoned: Several flea beetle species (potato, tobacco, and palestriped among them) that feed on pepper foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. NC State rates them minor pests of pepper, but they can set back small transplants badly.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks on seedlings, an organic spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating helps.
seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering so pollinators can reach the blooms. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay. Mature plants rarely need treatment.

beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter. A border of nasturtiums can lure them away.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until the soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults. A nasturtium trap planting at the bed edge can draw beetles off the crop.

beginner: Small pinprick scars appear on the pepper skin, and inside a maggot tunnels into the seed core, so the pepper ripens early and rots. It is mostly a problem in the Northeast. Good news for jalapeno: thin-walled hot peppers like it are rarely bothered, unlike thick bell peppers.
seasoned: A tiny white oviposition scar dimples the fruit surface where the fly laid an egg, and the maggot tunnels into the seed core inside; infested peppers often color up (turn red) prematurely and begin to rot from within. It is mainly a Northeastern and Mid-Atlantic pest, worst near tree lines. A useful jalapeno note: damage is negligible on slender, thin-walled peppers such as jalapeno and other hot types, which the maggot largely bypasses in favor of thick-walled bells.

beginner: The larva of a small fly that lays eggs inside pepper fruit in midsummer, mostly in the Northeast. The maggot eats the seed core. It prefers thick bell peppers, so jalapeno is rarely a target.
seasoned: The pepper maggot (Zonosemata electa), the larva of a striped fly that lays eggs in developing pepper fruit in July. Larvae feed inside the pod, then drop to the soil to pupate. Its host preference runs to thick-walled peppers, so hot, thin-walled types like jalapeno suffer little.

beginner: There is no easy fix once the maggot is inside the fruit, so the main tools are covering plants with insect netting in mid-July when the flies lay eggs and picking off any scarred, prematurely reddening fruit. Jalapeno is rarely affected, so most growers need no action.
seasoned: Because eggs and larvae are protected inside the fruit, control targets the adult fly, and insecticides are the only reliable option where the pest is established. In a home garden, covering plants with insect netting during the mid-July egg-laying window and removing infested fruit are the practical non-chemical tools.

beginner: Move peppers away from where they grew last year, clear weeds in the nightshade family nearby, and if pepper maggot is common where you live, cover plants with insect netting in mid-July. Growing jalapeno rather than thick bell peppers largely sidesteps this pest.
seasoned: Rotate peppers well away from last year's crop, control solanaceous weeds such as horsenettle that host the fly, cover the crop with insect netting during the mid-July egg-laying period, and disc or clear pepper residue promptly after harvest to kill larvae and pupae. Growing hot, thin-walled types like jalapeno is itself a strong cultural defense.

beginner: Flower buds and small peppers turn yellow and fall off, and any pods that hang on are black and full of grubs and debris inside. The culprit is a tiny dark beetle. It is mainly a problem in the warm South and Southwest.
seasoned: Small buds and young fruit yellow and drop, and cut pods reveal a grub feeding at the seed core, the inside turned black and filled with frass. The adult is a small dark, brassy-lustered weevil about an eighth of an inch long. It is a serious pepper pest of the South and Southwest (including Florida, Texas, and southern California) and cannot overwinter where winters are cold.

beginner: A tiny beetle whose grubs grow up inside pepper buds and fruit, causing them to drop or rot from the inside. It lives year-round in warm areas and comes in from weeds and old pepper plants.
seasoned: The pepper weevil (Anthonomus eugenii), whose larvae develop inside buds and pods. Females lay eggs in flower buds and young fruit; the grubs feed at the seed core, causing bud and fruit drop and internal contamination. It breeds continuously in warm regions and reinvades from nightshade weeds and volunteer peppers.

beginner: The main defense is cleanup: pick up and throw away every dropped or damaged pepper, since the grubs finish growing inside them, and check new plants before buying. Pull and destroy the plants as soon as harvest ends.
seasoned: Field sanitation is the core tool: remove and destroy dropped and culled fruit through the season, since larvae mature inside them, and inspect transplants so you do not bring the weevil in. Pheromone-baited sticky traps detect it early. In a home garden, destroying spent plants right after harvest sharply reduces the next year's population.

beginner: Do not plant peppers where they grew last year, clear out nightshade weeds and any leftover pepper plants nearby, buy healthy transplants, and clean up the garden as soon as the season ends.
seasoned: Rotate away from last year's peppers, remove nearby nightshade weeds and volunteer pepper and eggplant that harbor the weevil, monitor with pheromone traps, source clean transplants, and destroy the crop promptly at season's end to break the continuous breeding cycle.

beginner: Leaves vanish overnight, leaving bare stems, with dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight.
seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots or the odd fruit, are stripped overnight, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprit is the big green tobacco (or tomato) hornworm, up to three and a half inches long, which blends into the stems and is easiest to find by its frass.

beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on pepper and tomato leaves mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage.
seasoned: Tobacco and tomato hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including pepper from midsummer on. A few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage given their size, though peppers are a secondary host to tomato.

beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.

beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.
seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.

beginner: The leaves get small dark, water-soaked spots that grow into brown patches with yellow edges, and badly spotted leaves yellow and fall, leaving fruit exposed. Rough, scabby spots also appear on the peppers. It is the most common serious pepper disease and spreads in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Small, water-soaked spots on the leaves enlarge into brown, angular, sometimes scabby lesions with yellow halos, and heavy infection yellows and drops the foliage, exposing fruit to sunscald. Raised, scabby, cracked spots also form on the fruit, ruining it for use. It is the most common and damaging bacterial disease of peppers, worst in warm, wet, splashy weather.

beginner: A bacterium carried on seed and old plant debris that spreads in splashing water and on hands and tools when plants are wet. It thrives in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Xanthomonas bacteria, carried on seed and in crop debris and spread by splashing water and handling wet plants. Warm, humid, rainy conditions favor it, and once established in a planting it is very hard to stop, so control is built on clean seed, resistant varieties, and keeping foliage dry.

beginner: You cannot cure a plant that has it, so remove badly spotted plants and keep your hands and tools off wet foliage. Copper sprays can slow it a little, but prevention is what counts.
seasoned: There is no cure for an infected plant; remove badly affected plants to slow spread, avoid working among wet plants, and where pressure is high, copper-based sprays can suppress it, though resistance to copper is common. Management is preventive.

beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, look for resistant varieties, do not plant peppers in the same spot each year, water the soil rather than the leaves, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.
seasoned: Start with certified, pathogen-free or hot-water-treated seed and disease-free transplants, choose resistant varieties, rotate peppers on a 2 to 3 year cycle out of solanaceous beds, water at the soil to keep foliage dry, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, and remove crop debris at season's end.

beginner: The leaves turn a patchy light-and-dark-green mosaic and may pucker or narrow, and the plant is stunted with fewer, smaller peppers. Several viruses cause this, mostly carried by aphids.
seasoned: Leaves show a mottled light-and-dark-green mosaic, often puckered, narrowed, or distorted, and the plant stunts and sets fewer, smaller, sometimes misshapen or ringspotted fruit. Several viruses (cucumber mosaic, tobacco mosaic, and pepper-specific mottle viruses) cause the syndrome, most of them spread by aphids moving from plant to plant.

beginner: Viruses spread mainly by aphids, and some by hands, tools, and even tobacco products. Once a plant is infected there is no cure.
seasoned: A group of plant viruses, chiefly cucumber mosaic virus and tobacco mosaic virus, transmitted by aphids and, for the tobamoviruses, mechanically on hands and tools and through infected seed and tobacco products. There is no cure once a plant is infected, so control is aimed at the aphid vectors and at clean seed and sanitation.

beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant, so pull and destroy it so aphids do not carry the virus to healthy plants. Control aphids, wash your hands, and do not touch peppers right after handling tobacco.
seasoned: There is no treatment for an infected plant; remove and destroy it promptly to cut the source of further spread, and control the aphids that move the virus. Wash hands and disinfect tools between plants, and do not handle peppers after using tobacco.

beginner: Look for virus-resistant varieties, control aphids, keep weeds down, wash your hands before handling plants, and remove any stunted, mottled plants quickly. Do not use tobacco around peppers.
seasoned: Choose resistant varieties (many carry virus resistance), use clean seed, control aphids with reflective mulch and by conserving natural enemies, manage nearby weed reservoirs, wash hands and tools, and remove infected plants early. Avoid tobacco use around the plants.

beginner: Plants suddenly wilt and die, often with a dark rotted patch on the stem at the soil line, and the fruit can rot too, sometimes with white fuzzy growth. It strikes in warm, soggy soil after heavy rain.
seasoned: Plants wilt and collapse suddenly, often with a dark, water-soaked lesion girdling the stem at the soil line, and roots rot; dark, firm, sometimes white-cottony rot also strikes the fruit. Caused by Phytophthora capsici, it flares in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions and after heavy rain or flooding, and can move fast through a bed.

beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing and running water, attacking pepper roots, stems, and fruit in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts.
seasoned: Phytophthora capsici, a soilborne water mold that thrives in saturated soil and spreads in splashing and running water. It survives in soil and debris for years and moves fast in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground, attacking roots, crown, and fruit.

beginner: Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage. There is no good home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is what matters.
seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly, and improve drainage immediately. There is no effective home-garden cure once plants collapse, so control is preventive and drainage-based.

beginner: Plant on raised beds so water drains away, avoid wet low spots, do not overwater, water at the soil, and rotate peppers away from tomatoes, eggplant, and squash. Look for resistant varieties if this disease is common where you live.
seasoned: Plant on raised, well-drained beds, avoid low spots that stay wet, choose resistant varieties where available, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, rotate away from solanaceous and cucurbit crops on a long cycle, and avoid overwatering, which is the single biggest trigger.

beginner: Sunken dark spots appear on the peppers, especially ripe red ones, spreading into rotting patches flecked with tiny pink or black dots. It is worst in warm, wet, humid weather.
seasoned: Sunken, circular, water-soaked spots develop on the fruit, especially ripening red fruit, enlarging into dark lesions dotted with concentric rings of pink-to-black spore masses that rot the pepper. It is chiefly a fruit-rot disease, favored by warm, wet, humid weather, and can carry over on infected seed and debris.

beginner: A fungus that rots pepper fruit, spread by splashing water and carried on seed and old plant debris. Ripe peppers are hit hardest, especially in wet weather.
seasoned: Colletotrichum fungi that infect the fruit and are spread by splashing water; the pathogen survives on infected seed, crop debris, and volunteer plants. Ripe and injured fruit are most susceptible, and long warm, wet spells drive outbreaks.

beginner: Pick off and throw away infected peppers right away, keep the fruit dry by watering at the soil, and harvest ripe peppers promptly instead of leaving them out in wet weather. Rotted fruit cannot be saved.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected fruit promptly to reduce spore load, and keep foliage and fruit as dry as possible. Where the disease is active a labeled fungicide can protect healthy fruit, but rotted fruit cannot be saved. Pick ripening fruit promptly rather than letting it sit in warm, wet weather.

beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, do not plant peppers in the same spot for a few years, water at the soil, keep fruit off the ground, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.
seasoned: Start with clean or treated seed and healthy transplants, rotate peppers out of the bed for 2 to 3 years, water at the soil, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, stake to keep fruit off the ground, and remove crop debris at season's end.

beginner: Give jalapeno about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day, and keep it even, since uneven watering while the plant is flowering drops the blossoms and causes rot on the bottom of the peppers. Plants in pots dry out much faster. Interestingly, letting a hot pepper run a little dry late in the season can make it hotter.
seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Peppers want steady, even moisture, and the water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set: swings from dry to soaked drop blossoms and cause blossom-end rot on the developing pods. Container plants dry out far faster and need closer attention. A note peculiar to hot peppers: a mild, deliberate water pull as the fruit ripens tends to raise the heat, so a hot pepper grown slightly lean and dry late in the season is often the hottest.

beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, soaking the soil down 6 to 8 inches so the roots grow deep. Keep it even: letting the soil go bone-dry and then flooding it stresses the plant, drops flowers, and causes rot on the bottom of the peppers.
seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit set, wetting the soil to a depth of at least 6 to 8 inches so the roots follow the moisture down. Even, deep watering sets and fills well-shaped pods; letting the soil swing from dry to saturated stresses the plant, drops blossoms, and invites blossom-end rot and root disease.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, with a soaker hose or by holding the hose at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent disease. If you must use a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off by evening. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist and warm.
seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves and splashing water spread the bacterial spot, anthracnose, and Phytophthora blight peppers are prone to. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so leaves dry before evening. A layer of mulch buffers soil moisture and warmth and blocks soil-borne spores from splashing onto the lower leaves and fruit.

beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or stems and fruit go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly. Overwatering is the main cause of the disease that suddenly kills peppers.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil starves the roots of oxygen and is the single biggest trigger for Phytophthora blight, which collapses peppers quickly on heavy ground.

beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry. A long dry spell while it is flowering drops the flowers and causes rot on the bottom of the peppers, though a short dry stretch late on can make hot peppers hotter.
seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is common in heat and not alarming, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Sustained drought during flowering and fruit set drops blossoms and gives small pods and leathery, sunken blossom-end rot on the fruit. A brief, mild dry spell late in ripening, by contrast, tends to concentrate heat rather than harm the crop.

beginner: Keep the seed tray evenly damp and warm while the peppers come up. Hot peppers are slow to sprout, so do not let the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seed-starting mix evenly moist and warm through germination; hot-pepper seed is slow to sprout and must not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp, not soggy. Let the top begin to dry before watering again.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on under lights with even, moderate moisture, easing off between waterings so the mix never stays saturated.

beginner: Soak the plant in well when you set it out, then keep the soil evenly moist as it takes hold. Mulch keeps the moisture and warmth steady.
seasoned: Water in thoroughly at transplant, then hold even moisture at the base as the plant establishes; mulch to buffer soil moisture and warmth.

beginner: Keep watering steady once flowers open, about 1 inch a week soaked in deep. Uneven water now drops the flowers and causes rot on the bottom of the peppers.
seasoned: Jalapeno wants a leaner, steady 1 inch a week soaked 6 to 8 inches deep, leaning higher through flowering and fruit set. Even moisture here sets well-shaped pods and prevents blossom drop; dry-to-soaked swings drop blossoms and cause blossom-end rot.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the pods fill out. Letting it go bone-dry and then flooding it drops flowers and causes rot, so keep it steady.
seasoned: Pod set through sizing is the water-critical window: steady moisture fills well-shaped pods and prevents blossom-end rot, while dry-to-saturated swings give small, misshapen fruit. Keep the soil evenly moist, and do not let it dry out between waterings while pods are sizing.

beginner: Interesting trick: letting jalapenos run a little dry as they ripen makes them hotter. So ease back on the water a bit late in the season if you want more heat, but do not dry the plant out completely, since it is still making peppers.
seasoned: A trait peculiar to hot peppers: a mild, deliberate water pull as the pods ripen tends to raise their heat, so a jalapeno grown slightly lean and dry late in the season is often the hottest. Ease off a little as pods color, but keep the plant producing rather than droughting it hard.

beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for jalapeno. It keeps the plant hydrated without spreading leaf and fruit disease.
seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for jalapeno, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also prone to leaf and fruit diseases spread by wet foliage and splash. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.

seasoned: The water-critical stretch runs from flowering through fruit set and sizing. beginner: You can pick jalapeno two ways. Or leave it on the plant two to three more weeks and let it turn red, which makes it sweeter and hotter. Two things surprise first-timers: peppers get hotter as they ripen and when the plant is stressed by heat or dryness, and the fine tan lines or netting that show up on the skin, called corking, are a normal sign of a ripe, well-grown pepper, not damage. Cut the peppers off with scissors or a knife, leaving a bit of stem, instead of pulling, and keep picking so the plant makes more. Left on the plant another two to three weeks, the same fruit ripens through to red, growing sweeter AND hotter as it matures. Two things surprise new growers and are worth knowing: heat rises with both maturity and stress, so a red pepper, or one grown hot and a little dry, is hotter than a well-watered green one; and corking, the fine tan or brown netting and stretch marks that appear on the skin, is a sign of a mature, fast-grown pepper prized in markets, not a defect or a disease. Cut fruit with shears or a knife leaving a short stem, rather than pulling, since a yanked branch tears easily, and pick regularly, since removing mature pods keeps the plant flowering and setting more. Wear gloves when picking and especially when cutting hot peppers: capsaicin, the compound that makes them hot, is an oil that clings to skin and burns painfully if it reaches your eyes, nose, or lips, so keep your hands away from your face and wash well afterward.

beginner: Jalapeno is the most popular hot pepper for home gardens, a warm-season plant (Capsicum annuum) grown for its firm, medium-hot peppers. You grow it just like a bell pepper: start it indoors, then set it out into warm soil after the last frost, because peppers barely grow until it is truly warm. The special thing about jalapeno is its heat, which comes from capsaicin inside the pod. That heat is not fixed: peppers get hotter as they ripen from green to red and when the plant is stressed by heat or a little dryness, so the very same plant can give mild or fiery peppers depending on how you grow and pick them. Two things surprise beginners: the tan lines (corking) on a ripe jalapeno are a good sign, not damage, and you can pick the peppers firm and dark green (the usual way, about 70 to 80 days after planting out) or leave them to turn red for more heat. Like tomatoes, jalapeno drops its flowers and stops setting fruit in extreme heat, above about 90°F days and 75°F nights, then starts again when it cools. Watch for aphids, flea beetles on young plants, hornworms, and, in the South, the pepper weevil, and for diseases like bacterial spot and Phytophthora blight, which you head off with clean plants, crop rotation, and watering the soil rather than the leaves. seasoned: Jalapeno is a warm-season fruiting vegetable (Capsicum annuum), the most popular hot pepper in American gardens, grown for its firm, medium-hot pods. Its culture is that of any pepper, close to a bell: a heat-loving, self-fertile, transplant crop set into warm soil after frost, growing slowly until the ground is truly warm, then bearing continuously through the summer. What sets it apart is pungency. Jalapeno carries capsaicin, roughly 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville units, produced in glands on the placenta inside the pod, and its heat is not fixed: it rises as the fruit ripens from green to red and as the plant meets stress, especially heat and a controlled water pull, so the same variety can be mild or fiery depending on how and when it is grown and picked. Two jalapeno-specific points reassure new growers: corking, the fine tan netting on a mature pod's skin, is a prized sign of quality, not a defect; and pods can be picked firm and dark green (the usual harvest, around 70 to 80 days from transplant) or left to ripen red for more heat and sweetness. Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and pauses fruit set when days climb above about 90°F and nights above 75°F, so in the hottest regions the crop splits into a spring and a fall flush around the peak of summer. Its pests are aphids (and the mosaic viruses they carry), flea beetles on seedlings, the pepper maggot (which largely spares thin-walled hot types), the pepper weevil in the South, and hornworms; its main diseases are bacterial spot, mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, and anthracnose, all held off by clean seed, rotation, warm well-drained soil, and dry foliage. Handle the harvest with gloves: capsaicin is an oil that burns skin and eyes.
